title: 'Daily Newswatch - 7 Oct 2026
body: 'The FBM KLCI rose 0.1% to 1,633 points on Tuesday due to positive regional sentiment, tracking gains across major Asian markets after Wall Street's tech-led rally overnight, although elevated US Treasury yields continued to cap risk appetite. Health Technology (+6.3%), Producer Manufacturing (+1.8%) and Health Services (+1.7%) led sectoral gains, driven by Nestle (+1.3%), Kuala Lumpur Kepong (+0.5%) and Petronas Chemicals (+0.2%). Market breadth was positive, with 664 gainers ahead of 450 losers, while 560 counters closed unchanged. Asian markets closed mixed on Tuesday as most bourses tracked Wall Street's tech-led rally, with Japan further supported by a strong government bond auction that eased yield concerns, while South Korea fell as chip heavyweights came under selling pressure amid worries over elevated bond yields. Japan's Nikkei 225 led regional gains (+1.1%), followed by Hong Kong's Hang Seng (+1.0%) and Taiwan's TAIEX (+0.2%), while South Korea's KOSPI fell 0.9%. Mainland China markets remained closed for the National Day holiday and will resume trading on Thursday. In South Korea, NonEnergy Minerals (-2.7%), Process Industries (-2.0%) and Producer Manufacturing (-1.8%) were the sectoral laggards, dragged by DH Autonex, Exicure Hitron and SG Global. In China, in their last trading sessions, the sectoral gains were led by Health Care (+2.9%), Consumer Staples (+1.7%) and Financials (+1.0%), with CanSino Biologics, Shanghai Model Organisms and Suzhou Novoprotein Scientific as the top performers. European stocks closed firmly higher Tuesday, led by banks, consumer discretionary and autos as sovereign yields' surge paused. Euro STOXX 50 and STOXX Europe 600 each added 0.5%, to 6,272 and 636. Long-dated euroarea yields mostly fell, especially in higher-debt economies, easing ECB antifragmentation intervention fears. Banks tracked rebounding credit: BNP Paribas jumped 2.5%; UniCredit, Santander and Deutsche Bank rose 1.5% each. Intesa Sanpaolo rebounded 1.3% as markets reassessed a potential Banca MPS acquisition's return impact. Schneider Electric sank 4.5% after agreeing to buy US software firm PTC for $22.6 billion. US stocks closed higher Tuesday, supported by heavyweight tech as surging bond yields paused, easing pressure on its credit outlook. The S&P 500 (+0.6%) and Nasdaq 100 (+0.5%) hit record highs, while the Dow gained 253 points. AI infrastructure and hyperscaler stocks mostly rose as fresh sector deals spurred speculative demand. OpenAI discussed $30 billion financing with UAE funds; Alphabet gained 0.3% before acquiring nuclear capacity from Constellation Energy (+12.2%). AMD jumped 2.8% as CEO Lisa Su signalled strong chip demand ahead. Microsoft rose 0.8%, Amazon 1.9% and Nvidia 0.1%. IMF: Cost-of-living crises have lasting impact on inflation expectations, poverty, IMF says 5.33% on Monday Sharp spikes in food and energy prices will likely become more common, the International Monetary Fund said, warning such crises drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability. IMF research released on Tuesday examined three decades of strategies used by governments to mitigate price surges, as well as a new economic model that accounts for the higher inflation experienced by poorer households, which spend a higher share of their budgets on daily necessities. (Reuters) US: Oil Rises as Mideast Risks Remain 5.33% on Monday Crude oil climbed toward $90 per barrel on Wednesday, recovering from five-week lows as persistent risks to Middle East energy flows overshadowed signs of rising supply from the region. Iran has intensified attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in recent days, with the UK Maritime Trade Operations reporting nine incidents so far this month. (Trading Economics) US: Trade deficit widens in August amid strong imports 5.33% on Monday The US trade deficit widened more than expected in August, driven by a surge in imports of goods amid robust domestic demand, keeping trade on track to again subtract from economic growth in the third quarter. The trade shortfall increased 13.7% to US$105.6 billion (RM431.5 billion), the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis and Census Bureau said on Tuesday. (Trading Economics) US: 10-Year Treasury Yield Softens from 24-Year High The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note was at 5.26% on Tuesday, pausing a surge that peaked at a 24-year high of 5.33% touched yesterday, tracking the momentary dip in wholesale fuel prices. Oil bids were tamed by signs that some laden tankers passed through the Strait of Hormuz. The 10-year yield has surged over 110bps this year as risks of higher rates from the Federal Reserve, soaring federal deficit spending, and increasing corporate debt supply triggered a plunge in demand for duration. (Trading Economics) US: Logistics Growth 2nd-Highest in 4 Years The US Logistics Managers’ Index increased to 70.2 in September 2026 from 66.6 in August. It is the second-highest reading in four years, behind only June’s reading of 71.1. A faster increase was seen for Inventory Levels (58.9 vs 52.8) and Inventory Costs (79.9 vs 78.6) which is also having a significant effect on the warehousing market. Asian markets closed mixed on Tuesday as most bourses tracked Wall Street's tech-led rally, with Japan further supported by a strong government bond auction that eased yield concerns, while South Korea fell as chip heavyweights came under selling pressure amid worries over elevated bond yields. Mainland China markets remained closed for the National Day holiday and will resume trading on Thursday. title: 'FBM KLCI Slips At Open As Budget 2027 Looms
body: 'The FBM KLCI opened slightly lower on Wednesday as investors remained cautious ahead of the tabling of Budget 2027, with the market continuing to search for fresh catalysts.  At 9.05am, the benchmark index fell 3.22 points to 1,630.13, remaining rangebound amid continued uncertainty.  Apex Securities said easing crude oil prices and expectations surrounding Budget 2027 could provide some support to the local market, although a stronger recovery would likely require fresh foreign fund inflows and clearer direction on bond yields and geopolitical developments.  “We stay cautious on the local bourse this week, as easing crude oil prices and Budget 2027 expectations may offer some support, but a stronger recovery will likely require fresh catalysts such as foreign fund inflows and clearer direction on bond yields and geopolitical developments,” it said in a note.  The research firm also remained cautious on near-term global risk appetite, noting that the current rally was narrowly led by technology stocks while bond yields remained near multi-decade highs.  It said equities could remain vulnerable if the US Federal Reserve adopts a more hawkish tone.  Banking counters were among the early decliners, with CIMB falling seven sen to RM7.63 and Hong Leong Bank losing eight sen to RM22.  Press Metal shed six sen to RM7.13.  Among actively traded stocks, Metronic was unchanged at 0.5 sen and Zetrix AI remained at nine sen, while Top Glove jumped five sen to 92.5 sen.  Glove makers also gained amid renewed optimism in the sector, with Supermax rising two sen to 48 sen, Hartalega adding five sen to RM1.17 and Kossan gaining two sen to RM1.27.

title: 'Draft Penang Structure Plan 2040: Who are they building for?
body: 'This plan, the draft Penang Structure Plan 2040, is already well in progress. It has been put up for public display and feedback – but chances are, most people in Penang are not even aware of it. Look at it closely, and you will see that it looks like a developers’ and contractors’ dream. Plenty of ‘jobs for the boys’. Lot of land reclamation sites all over – about 12 from the looks of it. That includes the ‘Penang Gateway’ (no. 9 on the map) reclamation project somewhere in Batu Ferringhi. The SRS-proposed Islands B and C in the south are still on the map – despite previous reports that the project would be scaled down to just one island (Island A or the ‘Silicon Island’). There’s another large reclamation site on the southeast of Penang Island. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member And look at the half a dozen reclamation sites on the mainland. In the Penang channel, there appears to be a conflict in putting an earmarked reclamation project inside a zone that is supposed to be gazetted as a marine sanctuary – the unique Middle Bank seagrass strip in the Penang channel. Who are they building for, when the birth rate in Penang has shrunk well below population replacement level? Seems to me that Greed has taken over. Check out a new coastal ring highway on the east coast (no. 1). The third crossing (the tunnel?) is still on the map (no 6). They never give up, do they? And look at all the reclamation and ‘development’ slated for the area around Jerejak Island (no 9). Why are they indicating a 150-metre contour line above sea level, when at present there is a limitation on development above 76 metres about sea level? It seems they want to allow development on hill slopes even exceeding 300 metres above sea level, almost all the way up, subject to risk assessments and conditions. More multi-billion ringgit LRT links here and there but I don’t see much in the way of a “better, cheaper, faster” bus rapid transit and tram network. And where are the water taxi routes? Remember, after 18 years since the change in government in 2008, we still don’t have a more detailed local plan, which governs the permissible development and zoning densities allowed in your neighbourhoods. Why is that? And all this while, most of the Penang public remain blissfully in the dark about what is in store for them. The views expressed in Aliran's media statements and the NGO statements we have endorsed reflect Aliran's official stand. title: 'Ex-secretary to PM's Graft Case: Temporary Passport Release for Shamsul Iskandar
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): Datuk Seri Shamsul Iskandar Mohd Akin, a former senior political secretary to the prime minister, has obtained the Sessions Court’s approval for the temporary release of his international passport to enable him to attend several overseas programmes this month. The passport had been surrendered to the court as an additional bail condition after he was charged with five counts of corruption. According to his supporting affidavit obtained by the media, Shamsul Iskandar applied for the permanent return of his passport to facilitate overseas travel in connection with his duties. He said he intends to travel to Frankfurt, Germany, to attend the Frankfurt Book Fair organised by Rex Education from Oct 7 to Nov 11. “Based on my involvement with the Madani Community Leadership Academy, my participation in the book fair aims to foster synergy between organisations and provide mutual benefits to both entities. “Therefore, this participation will provide valuable international exposure to support and strengthen ongoing grassroots initiatives aimed at empowering civil society in line with the Madani principles, particularly through the promotion of literacy, leadership and knowledge,” he said in the affidavit. Shamsul Iskandar also said he had registered to attend the fifth AlBaraka Summit, themed Ethics in Action: Rebuilding Foundations and Advancing the Global Impact of the Islamic Economy, in London scheduled for Oct 13 and 14. He said the summit aims to strengthen ethical foundations for Islamic financial and non-financial institutions, governance systems and market practices. Shamsul Iskandar also said he plans to attend programmes in Ireland, as well as Bosnia and Herzegovina, in November and December. During Monday's proceedings, lawyer Yusmadi Yusoff, representing Shamsul Iskandar, told Sessions Court judge Suzana Hussin that his client had filed an application on Sept 30 for the permanent return of his passport. He also sought its temporary release to enable Shamsul Iskandar to attend programmes in Frankfurt and London this month. Deputy public prosecutor Julaila Jamaludin objected to the application for the permanent return of the passport, saying the supporting documents consisted only of an invitation letter and that the discussions could be conducted online. However, she did not object to the application for its temporary release. Suzana subsequently allowed the temporary release of Shamsul Iskandar’s passport, effective from Monday, on condition that it be returned to the court on or before Oct 16. The court also ordered the prosecution to file an affidavit in reply to the application for the permanent return of the passport by Oct 19, with the decision on the application set for Dec 8. Shamsul Iskandar, 51, faces two charges of agreeing to accept RM140,000 in cash from businessman Tei Jiann Cheing, also known as Albert Tei, as an inducement to assist a company owned by Tei in obtaining approval for a mineral exploration licence in Sabah. He also faces two charges of obtaining furniture and electrical appliances worth RM14,580.03 and RM22,249 respectively, from Tei for the same purpose. The offences were allegedly committed at premises in Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya, and a hotel car park in Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, as well as at Jalan P14A 1/1, Precinct 14, Putrajaya, between Nov 24, 2023, and March 5, 2024. In a separate charge, Shamsul Iskandar is accused of obtaining gratification amounting to RM64,924 from Tei, allegedly deposited into a CIMB Bank account belonging to Rahmalidya Buyong to cover the rental of a house in Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya, in exchange for assisting Tei's company in securing approval for a mineral exploration licence in Sabah. All five charges were brought under Section 17(a) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2009 (Act 694) and are punishable under Section 24(1) of the same Act, which provides for a maximum prison sentence of 20 years and a fine of at least five times the amount or value of the gratification, or RM10,000, whichever is higher, upon conviction. title: 'Autopsy Confirms Yong Peng Schoolgirl Died From Head Injury — Police
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): An autopsy on 16-year-old Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, who was believed to have been murdered at a school in Yong Peng, Johor, on Saturday, found that she died from blunt trauma to the head. Bukit Aman Criminal Investigation Department director Datuk M Kumar said the post-mortem was conducted on Sunday by a pathologist from the Forensic Department of Sultanah Nora Ismail Hospital in Batu Pahat. “A 16-year-old boy was arrested on Oct 3 and has been remanded for six days until Oct 9 to assist investigations,” he said in a statement Monday. Kumar said the case was being investigated for murder under Section 302 of the Penal Code, with the school and Education Ministry giving police their full cooperation. He assured that the investigation would be conducted thoroughly, transparently and professionally, with no attempt to cover up the case or protect any party. “The case is still under investigation. The public is advised not to speculate or make comments that could interfere with the investigation or manipulate facts with the intention of causing public anxiety,” he said. Irene Sofiya was found unconscious and covered in blood in the school hall at about 5.50pm on Saturday. The suspect was arrested in the Yong Peng at about 7pm the same day. title: 'UK Job Slump Longer Than During Financial Crisis, PMI Says
body: '(Oct 5): Britain’s jobs market is stuck in its longest downturn since the early 2000s, according to a closely-watched survey, surpassing the decline during the financial crisis. S&P Global’s UK purchasing managers’ index (PMI) said employers cut back on staff for a 24th consecutive month. The figures will be a concern for Andy Burnham’s government ahead of the budget later this month with the intensifying energy shock and artificial intelligence (AI) threatening to dampen demand for workers. Employers have been shedding staff since the Labour government raised payroll taxes and the minimum wage shortly after returning to power in 2024. There were some signs of the slump bottoming out, however, as job cuts in the services sector were the smallest in almost a year. Furthermore, Britain’s official unemployment rate remains much lower than during the period after the global financial crisis. Britain’s labour market has been soft despite the wider economy smashing expectations during a resilient first half of the year. S&P’s survey suggested that the private sector is largely holding up against the energy shock for now, with demand boosted by stronger consumer spending and technology services amid a rush to harness AI. The composite PMI eased to 52 in September from 52.5 the previous month, remaining above the 50 threshold separating growth from contraction. It was slightly better than the 51.7 reading in the flash estimate. Still, the outlook has darkened since a resurgence in energy prices last month that has prompted traders to ramp up bets on the Bank of England raising interest rates several times to stop inflationary pressures spreading across the economy. “Subdued demand conditions and rising inflationary pressures contributed to weaker business activity expectations for the year ahead,” said Tim Moore, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence. “Greater-than-expected business requirements seem to have helped to stem the jobs downturn in recent months.” The survey pointed to price pressures growing. Firms’ cost burdens and the prices they charge customers both rose at the quickest pace since June. title: 'Saudi, UAE to Cooperate in Building Crude Stockpile in Asia — Report
body: 'TOKYO (Oct 5): A framework for Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to cooperate with Asian countries on oil stockpiling is set to be launched, with Japan supporting the initiative through financial assistance and stockpiling expertise, the Nikkei business daily said on Monday. Saudi, UAE to cooperate in building crude stockpile in Asia, Nikkei reports The Japan-led Asia Zero-Emission Community (Azec), a grouping of 11 countries including Southeast Asian nations, will hold a ministerial meeting in the Philippines on Thursday, where senior Saudi and UAE officials are expected to announce their intention to cooperate on oil stockpiling, the Nikkei said. The framework is expected to be included in a joint statement from the meeting, providing a basis for member countries to discuss expanding oil reserves with Middle Eastern producers, it said Specific details and the scale of cooperation will be worked out through bilateral discussions with Saudi Arabia and the UAE possibly expanding exports to participating countries or providing priority supplies in an emergency, Nikkei said Japan already leases domestic private storage tanks to state-owned oil companies in countries such as Saudi Arabia under a joint stockpiling scheme, which Japanese companies can access in an emergency Japan is expected to share the framework at a ministerial dialogue of the International Energy Forum in Saudi Arabia on Oct 11, the report said. A Japanese industry ministry official who spoke on condition of anonymity confirmed there will be dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the UAE and oil-consuming countries in Asia on the sidelines of the Azec ministerial meeting, although no concrete projects will be discussed. title: 'Court allows temporary release of Shamsul Iskandar’s passport
body:
'

The Sessions Court has granted the temporary release of former PM’s political secretary Shamsul Iskandar’s passport for travel to Germany and London.

KUALA LUMPUR: Datuk Seri Shamsul Iskandar Mohd Akin, the former senior political secretary to the Prime Minister,  has obtained the Sessions Court’s approval for the temporary release of his international passport to enable him to attend several overseas programmes this month.

The passport had been surrendered to the court as an additional bail condition after he was charged with five counts of corruption.

According to his supporting affidavit obtained by the media, Shamsul Iskandar applied for the permanent return of his passport to facilitate overseas travel in connection with his duties.

He said he intended to travel to Frankfurt, Germany, to attend the Frankfurt Book Fair organised by Rex Education from Oct 7 to Nov 11.

“Based on my involvement with the Madani Community Leadership Academy, my participation in the book fair aims to foster synergy between organisations and provide mutual benefits to both entities.

“Therefore, this participation will provide valuable international exposure to support and strengthen ongoing grassroots initiatives aimed at empowering civil society in line with the MADANI principles, particularly through the promotion of literacy, leadership and knowledge,” he said in the affidavit.

Shamsul Iskandar also said he had registered to attend the fifth AlBaraka Summit, themed Ethics in Action: Rebuilding Foundations and Advancing the Global Impact of the Islamic Economy, in London scheduled for Oct 13 and 14.

He said the summit aimed to strengthen ethical foundations for Islamic financial and non-financial institutions, governance systems and market practices.

Shamsul Iskandar also said he planned to attend programmes in Ireland, as well as Bosnia and Herzegovina, in November and December.

During today’s proceedings, lawyer Yusmadi Yusoff, representing Shamsul Iskandar, told Sessions Court Judge Suzana Hussin that his client had filed an application on Sept 30 for the permanent return of his passport.

He also sought its temporary release to enable Shamsul Iskandar to attend programmes in Frankfurt and London this month.

Deputy Public Prosecutor Julaila Jamaludin objected to the application for the permanent return of the passport, saying the supporting documents consisted only of an invitation letter and that the discussions could be conducted online.

However, she did not object to the application for its temporary release.

Judge Suzana subsequently allowed the temporary release of Shamsul Iskandar’s passport, effective today, on condition that it be returned to the court on or before Oct 16.

The court also ordered the prosecution to file an affidavit in reply to the application for the permanent return of the passport by Oct 19, with the decision on the application set for Dec 8.

Shamsul Iskandar, 51, faces two charges of agreeing to accept RM140,000 in cash from businessman Tei Jiann Cheing, also known as Albert Tei, as an inducement to assist a company owned by Tei in obtaining approval for a mineral exploration licence in Sabah.

He also faces two charges of obtaining furniture and electrical appliances worth RM14,580.03 and RM22,249, respectively, from Tei for the same purpose.

The offences were allegedly committed at premises in Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya, and a hotel car park in Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin, as well as at Jalan P14A 1/1, Precinct 14, Putrajaya, between Nov 24, 2023, and March 5, 2024.

In a separate charge, Shamsul Iskandar is accused of obtaining gratification amounting to RM64,924 from Tei, allegedly deposited into a CIMB Bank account belonging to Rahmalidya Buyong to cover the rental of a house in Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya, in exchange for assisting Tei’s company in securing approval for a mineral exploration licence in Sabah.

All five charges were brought under Section 17(a) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2009 (Act 694) and are punishable under Section 24(1) of the same Act, which provides for a maximum prison sentence of 20 years and a fine of at least five times the amount or value of the gratification, or RM10,000, whichever is higher, upon conviction.

title: 'End ongoing violations of Orang Asli land rights in Pahang – 19 NGOs
body: 'We, the undersigned civil society organisations and individuals, are deeply concerned by the situation confronting the Orang Asli of Pahang in general, and of the communities of Tasek Bera in particular, who are facing eviction, harassment and arrest and are being treated as a scapegoat for ongoing deforestation. Violations in Tasek Bera In June 2026, about 20 Orang Asli villages in the Tasek Bera area received eviction notices from the Pahang Forestry Department, ordering them to vacate their settlements and farmland. These kampungs, including Kampung Kuala Serting, Kampung Lubuk Tiang, Kampung Tambangan, Kampung Lenguin, Kampung Gakuyah, Kampung Pathir, Kampung Limbahan, Kampung Mahang, Kampung Ibam and Kampung Buloh Nipis, lie within the Tasek Bera permanent forest reserve (hutan simpan kekal). In response, the communities acted collectively, erecting blockades to protect their customary lands and monitoring activities within their territories. On 14 September, officers from the Pahang State Forestry Department and Department of Wildlife arrived at Kampung Pathir, stating their intention to conduct land surveying. The communities refused them entry pending a resolution on the eviction notices, with Tok Batin Amir Noor Tan of Kampung Pathir calling for the eviction notices to be withdrawn. This standoff escalated, resulting in the arrest of five Orang Asli, four of them women, on the same day. These recent developments are not an isolated case and form part of a growing trend of land grabs in Pahang. For example, outside Tasek Bera, on 9 February, 21 Orang Asli villagers from Kampung Jemeri in Rompin, Pahang, were detained by police following a complaint from a company claiming rights to develop land allegedly owned by the sultan of Pahang. According to a community statement, the sultan had [allegedly] obtained title to the 718-hectare oil palm plantation, developed by Orang Asli smallholders, less than a month earlier, on 26 January. The land in question forms part of the traditional territories of Jakun smallholders who had opened their smallholdings there 10-13 years ago. Orang Asli not driving deforestation Since early 2026, we have observed the development of a narrative in Pahang portraying the Orang Asli as groups that are scheming with outsiders to convert forest reserves into agricultural land. For example, while the above events were occurring in Tasek Bera, mainstream and state media repeatedly circulated claims that more than 7,000 hectares of forest within the Tasek Bera Ramsar site, which spans 38,446 hectares, had been illegally converted. This conversion was attributed to six Orang Asli families who allegedly used outsiders to exploit customary land rights in carrying out the encroachment. This narrative fails to accurately depict the drivers of deforestation in the state. A recent article by RimbaWatch found that at least 72,000 hectares of forest are under threat in Pahang, driven primarily by the expansion of monoculture industrial timber plantations in forest reserves, a programme supported by both the state and federal governments. Measured against this scale, traditional forest utilisation carried out by Orang Asli communities is minor. Yet it is their communities, not state and corporate drivers of deforestation, that are being singled out and blamed. Orang Asli traditional territories have existed for generations, predating independence and their later gazettement as timber production areas. Research has continuously shown that safeguarded Indigenous territories exhibit remarkable ecological resilience and biodiversity outcomes. Arrests of Orang Asli community members, ongoing harassment and the undue stress of receiving eviction notices or discovering that their land now belongs to outsiders all point to a troubling reality: as rights to their traditional territories are denied, the Orang Asli in Pahang are becoming outsiders on their own territories and scapegoated as drivers of widespread deforestation. Apex courts’ consistent rulings The Federal Court and Court of Appeal have repeatedly recognised that Orang Asli possess native customary land rights – a form of proprietary right protected under Article 13 of the Federal Constitution, provided a substantial connection to the land in question can be proven [Rosli Jendut & Ors v Agrobest (M) Sdn Bhd & Ors (2026)]. These rights pre-date both the Aboriginal Peoples Act 1954 and the National Land Code, and do not depend on any document of title. The rights are not limited to settlement areas. As the Federal Court in Rosli Jendut makes clear, these rights also extend to lands which are central to the Orang Asli’s cultural way of life, such as tombstones and grave sites. As such, despite the lack of gazettement and formal documents of title, the proprietary rights of Orang Asli communities in Tasek Bera over their traditional territories should be recognised and respected according to the Federal Court. Call to action The gaps between the judiciary and the executive are glaring and deeply concerning. While the courts have, time and again, affirmed the proprietary rights of the Orang Asli to their traditional territories, this recognition is not reflected by executive action. Communities like the Orang Asli in Tasek Bera, while actively fighting to protect their territories, are bearing the cost of this disconnect through evictions, arrests and the destruction of their lands. We urge the federal government to intervene immediately to safeguard the rights and wellbeing of the Orang Asli, as recognised by our Federal Courts and the Constitution. We call for an end to the misleading and negative portrayal of the Orang Asli community. Furthermore, we call for the following measures. - The Pahang state government must withdraw all eviction notices issued to the Orang Asli communities in Pahang, particularly those grounded solely on the claim that the communities are residing within permanent forest reserves. - The Pahang state government and their agencies must conduct genuine free, prior and informed consent consultation with affected communities for any decisions that will affect them, in line with Malaysia’s commitments under the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). - Suhakam must conduct an independent inquiry into the conduct of the Tasek Bera enforcement operations, and the findings made public and acted upon by the federal and Pahang state government without delay, vis-a-vis recommendations made in the 2013 National Inquiry on the Land Rights of Indigenous Peoples in Malaysia being adopted and implemented. - The Pahang state government and its agencies (eg Jakoa) must accelerate and make transparent the gazettement of Orang Asli traditional territories, with clear timelines for the villages still pending survey. - The federal government must halt the ongoing amendment process of the Orang Asli Act 1954 until legally binding recognition of traditional territories is guaranteed. title: 'Bursa Malaysia gains on Wall Street lead as weak US payrolls temper Fed rate hike expectations
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Bursa Malaysia opened higher on Monday, tracking Wall Street’s gains after softer US payroll growth eased expectations of an immediate Federal Reserve rate increase. At 9.10 am, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) rose 5.01 points, or 0.31 per cent, to 1,635.88 from last Friday’s close of 1,630.87. The index opened 2.55 points higher at 1,633.42. On the broader market, gainers surpassed losers 224 to 158, with 337 counters unchanged, 2,054 untraded and 24 suspended. Turnover stood at 206.30 million shares worth RM98.78 million. Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the US 10-year yield remained elevated at 5.28 per cent and Brent crude oil settled at US$102.25 per barrel, keeping sentiment sensitive to interest rates and West Asia developments. “Over in Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index slipped below 24,000 as financial and technology shares weakened. “Back home, following FBM KLCI’s higher close last Friday, we anticipate tentative stabilisation within 1,625-1,635 today, with bargain hunting offering some support amid a cautious market undertone,” he told Bernama. Among the heavyweights, Maybank, Public Bank, CIMB and Tenaga Nasional gained four sen each to RM10.06, RN4.70, RM7.69, and RM13.00, while IHH Healthcare decreased six sen to RM7.74. In active trade, VS Industry added three sen to 32 sen, Notion VTec increased four sen to 74.5 sen, GB Bond inched up half-a-sen to 23.5 sen, SFP Tech gained a sen to 28.5 sen, while Dagang NeXchange was flat at 51.5 sen. Among the top gainers, Samaiden put on 19 sen to RM3.03, UWC was 16 sen firmer at RM7.73, Critical Holdings perked up 15 sen to RM2.61, Mi Technovation strengthened nine sen to RM5.30, and Solarvest advanced eight sen to RM4.25. Nestle led the decliners, falling 32 sen to RM89.20, while Vitrox eased 14 sen to RM10.32, Kobay Technology was 12 sen lower at RM2.18, Kelington shed five sen to RM8.58, and YTL Power International edged down four sen to RM5.64. On the index board, the FBM Mid 70 Index gained 28.14 points to 17,510.07, the FBM Emas Index appreciated 33.81 points to 12,204.38, the FBM Top 100 Index widened 32.24 points to 11,989.92, the FBM Emas Shariah Index advanced 22.28 points to 12,082.60, and the FBM ACE Index improved 31.41 points to 5,560.87. Sector-wise, the Industrial Products and Services Index inched up 0.59 of-a-point to 179.11, the Energy Index gained 2.57 points to 835.60, the Financial Services Index jumped 97.59 points to 19,138.10, and the Plantation Index gained 2.23 points to 9,058.78. — Bernama

title: 'This article first appeared in City & Country, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026
body: 'It was a scorching afternoon when Country Garden Pacificview Sdn Bhd (CGPV) executive director and chief of regional industrial business development Kevin Li and regional vice-president Syarul Izam Sarifudin arrived at The Edge ’s office in Petaling Jaya, Selangor. The pair had flown in from Johor Bahru to give an update on Forest City, a high-profile project in Johor that has dealt with some hot issues since its inception.  “What we achieved [since 2015] up to 2025 was merely concentrating more on our operational stability, resource integration and preparing for our next phase of growth,” says Syarul. “In the early years, we were primarily viewed as a residential real estate developer. But we are now embarking into a new sector — managing townships and driving actual economic nodes of financial and industrial development in southern Johor.”  The master developer of Forest City is a joint venture between China-headquartered developer Country Garden Holdings Co Ltd and Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd.  Operating as an independent local management unit under Country Garden Malaysia’s executive umbrella, CGPV is responsible for Forest City’s master plan development and management, industrial park development and Special Financial Zone (SFZ) operation.  Officially launched by the Malaysian government with duty-free island status in 2016, the 7,500-acre integrated development covers four reclaimed man-made islands over 5,000 acres and 2,500 acres on the mainland. Located in Iskandar Puteri, it sits along the Straits of Johor near the Malaysia-Singapore Second Link, just 2km across the water from Singapore.  The ambitious development has made international headlines over the years, some of them for the wrong reasons, especially since it has fallen short of market expectations in terms of progress, sales and occupancy rates. These challenges were compounded by the Covid-19 pandemic and the well-documented financial restructuring of its parent company amid China’s broader real estate liquidity crisis.  “When China’s property market faced a systemic downturn, amplified by global supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic shifts and strict pandemic controls, Country Garden — once China’s top property developer — was caught in the crossfire, just like many other big players in the country. However, late last year, our parent group successfully executed onshore and offshore debt restructurings in China,” says Li, who is also the chief financial officer of Country Garden Malaysia.  Regardless of the situation faced by its parent company, he highlights that Country Garden Malaysia operates with complete operational and financial independence.  “Since Country Garden entered Malaysia as its first overseas destination back in 2010 and 2011, the local operation has relied on an independent management team. For the past three years, our cash flow has been generated entirely within the country, allowing us to remain self-sustaining in terms of liquidity and debt servicing,” he says, adding that all five of its projects in the Klang Valley and Johor are performing steadily.  According to Li, Country Garden Malaysia’s sales and cash collection was RM1.3 billion in 2023, more than RM1.1 billion in 2024, and RM1.3 billion in 2025.  “More crucially, we utilised our local cash flows to fully settle bank borrowings and capital market obligations worth about RM2 billion over the past three years, including a RM1 billion sukuk … As at earlier this year, the remaining outstanding amount [of the sukuk] was only RM150 million. We pre-repaid them as our cash flow was comfortable.”  With most of its debts cleared, local rating agency RAM upgraded Country Garden Malaysia’s outlook rating from negative to stable in March, reflecting its balance-sheet resilience despite global sector volatility.  That financial stability has been supported by developments on the legal front. Malaysian courts have recently upheld the validity of sales and purchase agreements in favour of the developer. Dismissing buyer suits seeking to void contracts for reasons such as media portrayals of the project as a “ghost town”, the courts established that market downturns and post-purchase regret do not constitute grounds for breach. The decisions shield CGPV against speculative contract cancellations and protect its revenue base.  “Forest City has completed and delivered 26,000 residential units so far. We understand that we cannot make every single person happy, and it is normal to receive feedback or complaints. We respect the buyers’ legal rights,” Li says.  “But we also have our internal KPIs [key performance indicators] to meet. We are pleased to share that customer satisfaction consistently hits above 95% in our surveys and polls. Generally, the majority of our 20,000 residents are happy to live here, or they wouldn’t choose to continue staying. This is evidenced by our growing population.”  A city waking up  Today, Forest City is home to around 20,000 people living in 66 completed blocks, over 770 acres of the approved 5,000-acre reclaimed island land bank.  “If you pass by from Iskandar Puteri towards Batam, you can see the lights on across the residential towers at night,” Syarul says. “It is a night-and-day difference compared with what people experienced immediately after the pandemic in early 2021.”  Demographics have shifted significantly, he adds. While buyers were once predominantly mainland Chinese, the current resident base is largely local Malaysians, many of whom commute daily to Singapore or work in nearby industrial parks, as well as expatriates of different nationalities.  “The township’s commercial pulse is also quickening,” says Syarul. “The Fisherman’s Wharf commercial street has seen steady footfall, with duty-free shops, eateries and premier banking facilities, including branches of Maybank and CIMB, with Affin Bank and AmBank joining the fold soon.”  Forest City attracts between 1.5 million and two million tourists annually. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore.  There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families.  “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says.  Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024.  Balaji’s private co-living and co-working hub at Marina Hotel drew hundreds of international digital nomads, crypto enthusiasts and tech workers.  However, in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) revoked the Network School operator’s business licence for breaching local licensing conditions. The management of the school clarified that CGPV operates solely as a commercial landlord, and that the developer is fully cooperating with the local authorities to ensure all commercial tenants adhere to the regulatory framework.  Strategic shift  Li says while Forest City’s master plan is unchanged, CGPV is shifting its focus towards commercial and industrial developments, in alignment with the government’s broader economic development plan for the state.  “We maintain the master plan as it is because, to us, it is still a very fantastic plan even after a decade. Of course, for such a mega development, you have to do it in phases, and there will be small twists and adjustments in between. But overall, we do not have plans to review the master plan. Now, we are embarking on the third phase of development. We foresee the entire master plan being completed only by 2040. It is now 12% to 13% developed,” says Syarul.  The biggest “twists and adjustments” to the master plan were its integration into the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and designation as an SFZ.  In August 2023, the government announced that Forest City would be designated as an SFZ to boost foreign investment, with incentives such as a 15% income tax rate for skilled workers and lower business operating costs. A year later, the government launched the tax incentive framework for the SFZ, which includes a zero tax rate for single family offices (SFO), a 5% corporate tax rate for fintech and global business services, and concessionary income tax rates.  In early 2025, Malaysia and Singapore signed a bilateral agreement to establish the JS-SEZ. Under the agreement, Forest City was formally incorporated as Flagship G, one of nine primary flagship zones within the 3,505 sq km economic zone.  “We started [the master plan] with residential and, maybe, this made people misunderstand that Forest City is focusing on high-rise residential developments. The SFZ designation puts us right back on track to [industrial projects],” says Li.  “Under the SFZ blueprint, the development is divided into two distinct functional zones, where the island component acts as a core financial services hub, focusing on single-family offices, fintech, foreign payment operating systems and back-office financial services. Meanwhile, the mainland focuses on smart logistics, high-tech manufacturing and global business services.”  To encourage direct investments in Forest City, the Malaysian government established the Iskandar Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J) at Forest City’s 42-storey primary office tower, Menara Delima Satu, to streamline the investment process. The centre houses 18 government agencies under one roof and acts as a single processing point for foreign investors.  “A key cornerstone of the SFZ is attracting family offices. The SC (Securities Commission) set an AUM (assets under management) threshold of RM30 million for family offices setting up in Forest City, a far more accessible entry point compared with Singapore’s S$15 million (RM47.9 million) requirement or Hong Kong’s HK$240 million (RM124.7 million) benchmark,” Li says.  Syarul stresses, however, that Malaysia is not competing with Singapore or Hong Kong in the SFO segment but is instead complementing them.  “It is about synergy. Under the SFZ rules, family offices in Forest City can invest up to 90% of their AUM globally. This means that investors can set up their operational base here in Forest City at one-third to one-fourth of the operational cost, while still leveraging Singapore’s capital markets just across the strait. It is very attractive to many family offices,” he explains.  Under the SFO Incentive Scheme guidelines issued by the SC, it is mandatory to establish a physical office in Forest City to qualify for and maintain SC approval and the accompanying 0% tax incentive.  According to Li, over 40 SFOs have secured physi­cal office space in Forest City, with nine having formally received SC approval to date.  “We are very positive about this, though we do not have an actual target of having many of them in Forest City in the near future because it is beyond our control and SC has its plan. But it is a strong catalyst in helping to add vibrancy to Forest City because when the offices come, they bring in their professional teams — accountants, lawyers and finance and investment experts,” he adds.  Forest City is also targeting global business services. CGPV is in advanced discussions with two major international banking institutions — one looking to relocate its back-office operations from Singapore, and another expanding its operational footprint from Kuala Lumpur.  Forest City 2.0  Despite the tailwinds from the SFZ, Li and Syarul acknowledge that transforming the mega project into a self-sustaining regional economy is not without immediate, real-world hurdles. The most pressing challenge currently is cross-border physical connectivity and accessibility.  “While the project is geographically proximate to Singapore, seamlessly moving people, goods and daily commuters across borders remains a complex, multi-jurisdictional effort,” says Li. “Furthermore, regional competition from peers like Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means that Malaysia must continually sharpen its execution speed and policy delivery to stay ahead.”  To close this connectivity gap, Country Garden is taking interim measures while lobbying government authorities for long-term infrastructure approvals.  “Before all the major government infrastructure projects are completed, we are bridging the gap ourselves. We currently run daily direct shuttles transferring residents and workers to the Sultan Abu Bakar CIQ Second Link complex,” Li says.  For the long term, the developer has submitted plans to the joint Malaysia-Singapore ministerial committee under the Iskandar Regional Development Authority (IRDA) for a dedicated ferry terminal. The developer is now planning subsequent sub-phases over a 10- to 12-year development cycle.  In Kuala Lumpur, the initial two phases of township development Lake City in Taman Wahyu are completed and sold out, with Phase 3 scheduled for launch next year. The remaining four parcels have been earmarked for development over a 15-year period.  In Semenyih, Selangor, residential development Diamond City launched its final landed parcel in September 2025, which is expected to wrap up construction within two years.  With a substantial land bank in its existing portfolio, the developer will focus its resources on executing its active pipeline over the next decade.  As the interview draws to a close, both Li and Syarul reflect on the long-term nature of master township development.  “Rome was not built in a day,” Li says. “When we first came to this coastal area in Johor, it was completely rural. Today, the infrastructure is firmly established. Development never moves in a straight upward line; it moves in spirals, but it always moves forward.  “We wish the public to know that since the first day Country Garden has been here in Malaysia, we have wanted to be here long term. Of course, there are twists and turns over the years, but we cannot deny the contribution of the company in Malaysia.”  He says Country Garden has invested RM32 billion in Malaysia, including RM20 billion in Forest City alone.  “We have created jobs, contributed to the country’s tax revenues and trained local skilled workers. Most importantly, after so many challenges and uncertainties, we were here, and we are still here today. The fundamentals are in place, and we have absolute faith in what Forest City will become.”

The decisions shield CGPV against speculative contract cancellations and protect its revenue base.  “Forest City has completed and delivered 26,000 residential units so far. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore.  There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families.  “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says.  Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024. title: 'CIMB Niaga siap perluas QRIS cross border ke Hong Kong dan Arab Saudi
body: 'KONTAN.CO.ID-JAKARTA. PT Bank CIMB Niaga Tbk terus memperluas layanan QRIS cross border seiring dengan pengembangan konektivitas pembayaran lintas negara oleh Bank Indonesia (BI).  Terbaru, CIMB Niaga menyatakan siap mengikuti perluasan QRIS cross border ke Hong Kong dan Arab Saudi.  Head of Digital Banking & Contact Center CIMB Niaga Lusiana Saleh mengatakan, perseroan akan mengikuti agenda BI untuk memperluas implementasi QRIS cross border ke kedua negara tersebut.  “Coming soon itu sudah dipatok sama BI, kita harus luncurkan itu. Oke, siap, kita akan luncurkan itu,” ujar Lusiana di Jakarta, Jumat (2/10).  Saat ini, CIMB Niaga telah mengimplementasikan QRIS cross border di sejumlah negara. Lusiana menyebut China dan Korea Selatan sebagai salah satu negara terbaru yang telah terhubung dengan layanan tersebut.  Menurut dia, penggunaan QR di China menjadi salah satu faktor yang mendukung perkembangan transaksi QRIS cross border CIMB Niaga di negara tersebut. Masyarakat China dinilai sudah terbiasa menggunakan pembayaran berbasis QR dalam transaksi sehari-hari.  “Proses kita di China mulai banyak, karena China itu juga negara QR, jadi secara otomatis orang terbiasa untuk menggunakan QR,” jelasnya.  Lusiana mengatakan, dari sisi kesiapan infrastruktur, CIMB Niaga tidak melihat adanya kendala berarti untuk mengikuti perluasan QRIS cross border.  Pasalnya, perseroan selama ini juga aktif mengikuti berbagai proyek percontohan yang dilakukan BI dalam pengembangan ekosistem pembayaran digital.  “Selama ini kita juga selalu mendukung Bank Indonesia, setiap tahun mereka piloting di beberapa negara pun, kita selalu ikutan,” kata Lusiana.  Selain QRIS cross border, CIMB Niaga sebelumnya juga turut berpartisipasi dalam pengembangan QRIS Tap dan implementasi tap in tap out pada layanan transportasi.  Dengan semakin luasnya konektivitas QRIS lintas negara, CIMB Niaga melihat peluang transaksi digital masih terbuka. Perseroan juga terus mendorong penggunaan transaksi nontunai di dalam negeri.  Lusiana mengatakan, QRIS saat ini menjadi salah satu transaksi digital dengan penggunaan tinggi di CIMB Niaga, diikuti transaksi transfer melalui BI-FAST.

title: 'Apa yang mesti berubah sebelum pelajar lain dicederakan?/ What must change before another child is hurt?
body: '[ENGLISH VERSION BELOW] Kematian Muhammad ldlan Fareeq Shahril, 14 tahun, meninggalkan sebuah keluarga dalam kesedihan dan ibu bapa di seluruh Malaysia dengan satu pertanyaan yang amat membimbangkan: adakah anak saya selamat di asrama sekolah? Bagi pihak Children’s Protection Society Malaysia (CPSM), saya merakamkan ucapan takziah yang sedalam-dalamnya kepada ibu bapa dan keluarga Muhammad ldlan. Tiada kata-kata yang dapat meringankan kehilangan mereka. Mereka berhak mendapat ruang untuk berduka, dan jawapan yang benar serta keadilan. Kami mengambil maklum bahawa Menteri Pendidikan Fadhlina Sidek telah bertemu dengan keluarga dan warga sekolah serta mengarahkan audit segera. Kami menyambut baik jaminan beliau bahawa tiada sesiapa akan dilindungi sekiranya salah laku terbukti. Polis mesti diberi ruang untuk menentukan fakta, termasuk punca dan keadaan yang membawa kepada kematian Muhammad ldlan. Dakwaan tidak boleh dianggap sebagai dapatan, dan pelajar yang terlibat tidak wajar dihakimi oleh masyarakat sebelum siasatan selesai. Namun, siasatan terhadap satu kejadian tidak boleh menjadi noktah kepada perkara ini. Audit tersebut perlu menjawab soalan yang lebih sukar: adakah terdapat kebimbangan yang timbul sebelum kematian Muhammad ldlan, dan adakah pihak asrama mempunyai cara yang berkesan untuk mengenal pasti serta menanganinya? Soalan ini perlu diteliti tanpa membuat andaian tentang apa yang berlaku dalam kes ini. Apabila seorang pelajar tinggal di asrama, pihak sekolah memikul tanggungjawab menjaganya pada waktu ibu bapanya tidak dapat melihat keadaannya sendiri. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Tanggungjawab itu melangkaui daftar penghuni dan peraturan yang ditampal pada papan kenyataan semata-mata. la memerlukan orang dewasa yang mengenali pelajar, menyedari perubahan tingkah laku, mengambil tindakan apabila kebimbangan dibangkitkan dan bertanggungjawab terhadap keselamatan mereka selepas waktu persekolahan. Tiada pelajar berhak menguatkuasakan disiplin dengan kekerasan. Jika seorang pelajar disyaki melanggar peraturan, sama ada berkaitan dengan vape, barang yang hilang, sikap tidak menghormati orang lain atau apa-apa perkara sekalipun, urusan itu mesti dikendalikan oleh orang dewasa yang bertanggungjawab. Pelajar tidak boleh ditampar, dipukul, ditahan secara paksa, diugut atau dikenakan hukuman yang dikendalikan oleh pelajar lain. Sesiapa yang melihat sesuatu masalah hendaklah melaporkannya kepada warden atau guru disiplin. Tiada tempat bagi pelajar yang melantik diri mereka sendiri sebagai penguat kuasa di dormitori, asrama atau sekolah. Oleh itu, CPSM menyeru Kementerian Pendidikan supaya menggunakan audit semasa sebagai permulaan kepada semakan keselamatan asrama yang jelas dan mempunyai tempoh pelaksanaan yang ditetapkan. Semakan itu perlu merangkumi perkara berikut. Pertama, teliti sama ada tanda amaran terlepas pandang. Penyiasat dan pasukan audit perlu meneliti aduan terdahulu, laporan tidak rasmi, permintaan untuk bertukar bilik, kecederaan yang tidak dapat dijelaskan, ketidakhadiran, perubahan tingkah laku dan kebimbangan yang dibangkitkan oleh ibu bapa, sekiranya maklumat tersebut wujud. English version A child died in a school hostel. What must change before another child is hurt? The death of 14-year-old Muhammad ldlan Fareeq Shahril has left a family grieving and parents across Malaysia asking a painful question: is my child safe in a school hostel? On behalf of the Children’s Protection Society Malaysia (CPSM), I extend our deepest condolences to Muhammad ldlan’s parents and family. No statement can lessen their loss. They deserve compassion, privacy, truthful answers and justice. We acknowledge that Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek met the family and school community and directed an immediate audit. We welcome her assurance that no one will be protected if wrongdoing is established. The police must be allowed to establish the facts, including the cause and circumstances of Muhammad ldlan’s death. We must not turn an allegation into a finding or expose the children involved to public judgement before the investigation is complete. But an investigation into one incident cannot be the end of the matter. An audit must answer a harder question: were there concerns before Muhammad ldlan’s death, and did the hostel have a reliable way to recognise and respond to them? That question must be asked without presuming what happened in this case. A hostel takes responsibility for children during the hours when their parents cannot see them. That responsibility extends beyond a register of occupants and a set of rules on a noticeboard. It requires adults who know the children to notice changes in behaviour, respond to concerns and remain accountable for what happens after classes end. No student has the authority to enforce discipline by force. If a student is suspected of breaking a rule, whether it concerns vaping, a missing item, disrespect or anything else, the matter belongs with responsible adults. A child must never be slapped, struck, restrained, threatened or subjected to a punishment devised by other students. A student who sees a problem should report it to a warden or disciplinary teacher. There is no place for self-appointed enforcers in a dormitory, hostel or school. The CPSM therefore calls on the Ministry of Education to use the current audit to begin a clear, time-bound review of hostel safety. That review should address the following. First, find out whether warning signs were missed. Investigators and auditors should examine earlier complaints, informal reports, requests to change rooms, unexplained injuries, absences, changes in behaviour and concerns raised by parents, where such information exists. They should establish who received each concern, what action followed, and whether anyone checked back with the child. A finding that no complaints were recorded would need to be considered alongside whether children had a safe and credible way to speak up. Second, put adult supervision where and when children need it. Wardens cannot provide careful oversight if they are responsible for too many students, buildings or duties at once. The ministry should review hostel staffing, night coverage, handovers and escalation arrangements. Every hostel should have an identifiable adult on duty, a clear arrangement for cover when that adult is unavailable, and a secure record of concerns raised and action taken. Third, give children a reporting route they can trust. A child should be able to speak privately to more than one designated adult, including someone outside the hostel’s daily chain of command. Parents must know whom to contact. Reports involving violence or threats must receive a prompt response, an assessment of the child’s immediate safety, protection against retaliation and follow-up. Children must be told plainly that reporting harm is an act of courage, not disloyalty. Fourth, understand each child’s needs at hostel intake. Schools should speak with students and parents about adjustment to hostel life, previous safety concerns and any support the child may need. Where a concern warrants further assessment, a qualified professional should be involved. Information gathered must be kept confidential and used to plan appropriate support and supervision, not to label a child or deny access to education on the basis of an untested assumption. Fifth, make the rule against violence a living practice. Principals, wardens, disciplinary teachers, counsellors and, where relevant, ustaz or other religious educators should reinforce the same message. Weekly assemblies and hostel meetings can provide regular opportunities to discuss boundaries, peer pressure, respectful correction and how to seek help. Zero tolerance must mean a consistent response to violence: taking every report seriously, protecting the children involved, establishing the facts and acting fairly. The instructions to students must be unmistakable: keep your hands off another child, report the issue to an adult, and intervene safely by getting help. Sixth, act on practical security measures. The ministry should review security arrangements across school hostels and identify shared areas where CCTV would strengthen oversight, with priority given to locations where children may be particularly vulnerable and adult supervision is limited. Cameras must respect children’s privacy and cannot replace attentive adults. Any system must have designated personnel responsible for checking that it works, responding to reported incidents and preserving relevant recordings before they are overwritten. Access to footage should be restricted and documented, with prompt provision to investigators through proper channels and safeguards for the children recorded. Accountability must extend beyond this case. The questions raised by this death must lead to action that parents and children can see. The ministry should publish the audit’s key findings as soon as it can do so, without compromising the police investigation or the privacy of the children involved. It should state what will be corrected, who is responsible and when each action will be completed. The review should then be extended to other hostels, with progress reported publicly. The wider messages children receive about violence also deserve attention. Creative industries and regulators should consider how bullying is portrayed to young audiences, particularly when intimidation appears powerful or free of consequences. Young people should be heard on the messages they take from what they watch. Such portrayals cannot explain Muhammad ldlan’s death; the facts of this case are for investigators to establish. The duty to keep children safe remains with the adults and institutions entrusted with their care. Parents entrust schools with their children, not merely their exam results. Muhammad ldlan’s family deserves the truth about what happened. Every child living in a hostel deserves a trusted adult to turn to and a system that responds before harm becomes irreversible. – CPSM Dato’ Seri Nazir Ariff is the president of the Children’s Protection Society Malaysia. The instructions to students must be unmistakable: keep your hands off another child, report the issue to an adult, and intervene safely by getting help. Sixth, act on practical security measures. The ministry should review security arrangements across school hostels and identify shared areas where CCTV would strengthen oversight, with priority given to locations where children may be particularly vulnerable and adult supervision is limited. Cameras must respect children’s privacy and cannot replace attentive adults. Any system must have designated personnel responsible for checking that it works, responding to reported incidents and preserving relevant recordings before they are overwritten. Access to footage should be restricted and documented, with prompt provision to investigators through proper channels and safeguards for the children recorded. Accountability must extend beyond this case. The questions raised by this death must lead to action that parents and children can see. The ministry should publish the audit’s key findings as soon as it can do so, without compromising the police investigation or the privacy of the children involved. It should state what will be corrected, who is responsible and when each action will be completed. The review should then be extended to other hostels, with progress reported publicly. The wider messages children receive about violence also deserve attention. Creative industries and regulators should consider how bullying is portrayed to young audiences, particularly when intimidation appears powerful or free of consequences. Young people should be heard on the messages they take from what they watch. Such portrayals cannot explain Muhammad ldlan’s death; the facts of this case are for investigators to establish. The duty to keep children safe remains with the adults and institutions entrusted with their care. Parents entrust schools with their children, not merely their exam results. Muhammad ldlan’s family deserves the truth about what happened. Every child living in a hostel deserves a trusted adult to turn to and a system that responds before harm becomes irreversible. – CPSM Dato’ Seri Nazir Ariff is the president of the Children’s Protection Society Malaysia. title: 'TNB Moving Higher Up The ESG Ladder
body: 'Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) is strengthening its environmental, social and governance (ESG) profile through major renewable energy and hydroelectric upgrades that align with Malaysia’s national energy transition agenda.  Following an investor webinar held by TNB on Oct 1, it was highlighted that the utility group’s Hybrid Hydro Floating Solar (HHFS) project at Tasik Kenyir and the Sungai Perak Hydro Life Extension Programme (HLEP) as two initiatives supporting the transition towards a lower-carbon electricity system.  Malaysia’s National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR) targets renewable energy accounting for 70% of installed power capacity by 2050, a target reaffirmed by the government as recently as September.  The first phase of the Kenyir project, known as Kenyir #1, will comprise 595MWac of floating solar capacity integrated with a 297.5MW battery energy storage system (BESS).  The engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning contract has been awarded to the Cypark-Sunview consortium, with commercial operations targeted for the fourth quarter of 2028.  TNB expects the project to generate a high single-digit equity internal rate of return, despite floating solar requiring around 10% to 15% higher capital expenditure than conventional ground-mounted solar.  The economics are supported by a 21-year Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS) offtake agreement with DayOne Data Centers, CIMB said.  From an ESG perspective, TNB highlighted several advantages of the floating solar project. These include higher power output from the cooling effect of the water body, the avoidance of land clearing and an estimated reduction of 650,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually.  The project is also expected to have limited impact on Tasik Kenyir’s biodiversity as the installation will occupy only about 1.4% of the lake’s surface area.  Alongside new solar capacity, TNB is investing RM5.8 billion in rehabilitating and upgrading its ageing Sungai Perak Hydroelectric Plant network.  The HLEP covers five hydroelectric stations with a combined installed capacity of 648MW. Progress had reached 36% as of June 2026, with commissioning scheduled progressively between 2026 and 2033.  Once completed, the plants are expected to operate for another 40 years under a new power purchase agreement, allowing TNB to preserve existing renewable generation assets while extending their productive lifespan.  CIMB said both initiatives fit with the NETR’s emphasis on expanding renewable generation and energy storage capacity. The roadmap identifies renewable energy as one of Malaysia’s core energy-transition levers.  The research house maintained its BUY call and RM15.90 target price on TNB, while keeping its FY2026-FY2028 core earnings forecasts unchanged.  CIMB does not expect the projects to provide a meaningful earnings boost over the next three years, given their development timelines, but views them positively for TNB’s longer-term sustainability positioning and said they could contribute to further improvements in the group’s ESG ratings.

title: 'Ibu janji ambil kami di sekolah, tapi dia pergi selamanya'
body: 'GUA MUSANG: Hancur hati dua beradik apabila ibu dinanti untuk menjemput pulang dari sekolah tidak kunjung tiba, sebaliknya berita duka diterima apabila insan tersayang itu meninggal dunia akibat kemalangan. Nur Arissa Najla Mohd Shazuam, 13, dan Nur Amani Nuwairah Mohd Shazuam, 15, menanti penuh sabar selepas ibunya, Nor Hasyikim Daud, 34, berjanji mengambil mereka pulang dari Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan (SMK) Bandar Chiku. Nur Arissa Najla berkata, dia menerima berita kemalangan itu daripada seorang rakan ketika menunggu pada 1.40 tengah hari. "Ibu ada maklumkan akan ke Gua Musang dengan rakannya dan berjanji mengambil saya serta kakak dari sekolah. "Pada hari kejadian, saya menduduki tiga kertas peperiksaan dan sangat teruja untuk memberitahu ibu yang saya boleh jawab semua soalan subjek Sejarah. "Lebih setengah jam menanti ibu, namun tidak kunjung tiba, sebaliknya saya terima berita ibu kemalangan. "Saya nampak bapa saudara datang menjemput kami," katanya ketika ditemui di Felda Chiku 5 di sini. Dalam kejadian Ahad lalu, Nor Hasyikim maut di lokasi kejadian apabila kenderaan dipandunya bertembung dengan lori 10 tan di Kilometer 40 Jalan Gua Musang-Kuala Krai. Mangsa meninggal dunia akibat tersepit, manakala rakannya di tempat duduk penumpang hadapan cedera parah. Allahyarham turut meninggalkan seorang bayi Nur Aireen Nisrina berusia 11 bulan. Sementara itu, kakak kepada Nor Hasyikim, Siti Noraeshah Daud, 39, berkata, tiga beradik itu akan dijaga ibunya dengan bantuan adik-beradik lain. "Sejak setahun lalu arwah membesarkan tiga anaknya dengan bekerja di kantin asrama SMK Bandar Chiku. "Selepas ini kami akan bersama-sama menjaga dan membesarkan tiga anak perempuan arwah," katanya. Orang ramai yang ingin memberi sumbangan boleh menyalurkan ke akaun Bank CIMB milik Siti Noraeshah Daud bernombor 7601845122.

title: 'Refugees are not ‘foreign fugitives’
body: 'Charles Santiago The Ministry of Home Affairs should be careful about the language it uses to describe Myanmar nationals in Malaysia. People who have fled genocide, conflict or religious persecution are not “foreign fugitives” simply because they lack regular immigration status. Immigration status and criminality are not interchangeable. The government says the repatriation programme is voluntary, orderly and based on individual consent. But a genuinely voluntary return requires more than a signature. People must be able to make an informed decision, free from coercion, with a proper assessment of the risks they face on return. It is particularly troubling that the UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, says it had no role in Malaysia’s repatriation process. It has also warned that Myanmar remains unsafe for refugee returns. Consultation needs to be transparent too. Where is the meaningful engagement with the UNHCR, Suhakam, refugee-led organisations and civil society groups that have worked directly with these communities for years? - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member These groups hold information about individual vulnerabilities, family circumstances, protection concerns and conditions in Myanmar. Government agencies cannot simply assume they know these things. If the government has carried out comprehensive screening and concluded that every person returned can safely go home, it should publish the methodology, safeguards and independent verification mechanisms behind that conclusion. And if the government’s justification is that Myanmar nationals are a ‘financial burden’ or a ‘security threat’, the people of Malaysia deserve evidence. What is the actual public expenditure? Which specific security threats are being referred to? Are they a bigger threat than the two million undocumented migrant workers who have been in the country for the past 20 years or so? This is not about asking Malaysia to abandon immigration enforcement or national sovereignty. It is about insisting that sovereignty and the rule of law operate alongside due process, evidence and protection from return to danger. The return of 1,476 people has now begun. That makes transparency and independent scrutiny even more urgent. It also makes it harder for Malaysia to claim the moral authority to speak forcefully about the forced displacement of Palestinians, or to champion refugee rights elsewhere. Vulnerable people are being returned to a country where they could face detention, torture, forced conscription or death. Charles Santiago is a prominent Malaysian politician, economist and human rights advocate who served three terms as the MP for Klang and has twice chaired the National Water Services Commission. title: 'DNB completes RM5.2b financing, unlocking next phase of 5G growth in Malaysia
body: 'PETALING JAYA: Digital Nasional Bhd (DNB) has completed a RM5.2 billion syndicated Islamic term financing exercise, a transaction that ranks among the largest syndicated loan facilities ever arranged for an unlisted company in Malaysia. DNB CEO Datuk Azman Ismail said, “The successful completion of this RM5.2 billion financing exercise marks a significant milestone for DNB and reflects strong confidence in our business fundamentals, operational track record and long-term role in Malaysia’s digital economy. “This financing provides DNB with a sustainable platform to operate on its own, continue investing in network enhancement and capacity expansion, and leverage our expanded spectrum assets. “As Malaysia progresses under the dual network framework, DNB remains committed to providing world-class digital infrastructure that supports our shareholders, customers, enterprises and government agencies. “With strong financing, enhanced spectrum resources and a proven nationwide 5G platform, DNB is well positioned to support the government’s AI Nation aspirations and help power Malaysia’s next phase of digital growth.” Maybank Investment Bank Bhd acted as mandated lead arranger, bookrunner and coordinating arranger with AmInvestment Bank Bhd, CIMB Islamic Bank Bhd, RHB Islamic Bank Bhd and United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd as joint mandated lead arrangers. AmInvestment Bank acted as financial adviser to DNB. This significant step marks DNB’s evolution as Malaysia transitions to the next phase of its dual 5G network framework. The financing strengthens DNB’s long-term financial position and facilitates the planned exit of Minister of Finance Incorporated (MOFInc) as an ordinary shareholder and the transition to equal ownership among its mobile network pperator shareholders, namely CelcomDigi Bhd through Infranation Sdn Bhd, Maxis Broadband Sdn Bhd and YTL Power International Bhd, expected in the early fourth quarter of 2026. MOF Inc will retain a special share in DNB to safeguard national interests, ensuring continued stewardship of key strategic matters while enabling the company to advance its next phase of development. The syndicated financing exercise includes the refinancing of DNB’s Government Guarantee Revolving Credit Facility, which expired on Sept 29, and establishes a sustainable long-term funding structure to support the company’s future growth. The completion of the financing coincides with the award of the full 100 MHz of the 3.3–3.4GHz spectrum and the conversion of DNB’s entire 240MHz spectrum holding to a spectrum assignment. Following the issuance of the spectrum assignment by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC), the assignment took effect yesterday, providing greater regulatory certainty and strengthening DNB’s ability to support Malaysia’s evolving 5G connectivity needs. The 240 MHz spectrum block will enhance network capacity, efficiency, and performance, enabling faster speeds, lower latency, and an improved customer experience. It also supports the deployment of advanced technologies, including Massive MIMO, carrier aggregation, 5G Advanced and AI-driven network capabilities, further strengthening DNB’s leadership in next-generation connectivity. Together, the financing and the spectrum assignment strengthen DNB’s ability to enhance network quality and resilience, support future demand, and advance Malaysia’s digital economy ambitions.

title: 'Bursa Ends Lower, FBM KLCI Sheds 20.81 Points As Selling Pressure Persists
body: 'Bursa Malaysia closed broadly lower on Oct 1, with the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) falling 20.81 points, or 1.26%, to 1,630.36 as continued selling pressure tracked a mixed and cautious Wall Street session overnight.  The benchmark index, which closed at 1,651.17 on Sept 30, traded between 1,630.10 and 1,649.87 during the day.  Weakness extended across the broader market. The FBM 70 dropped 215.69 points, or 1.23%, to 17,358.98, while the F4GBM fell 12.12 points, or 1.22%, to 984.34.  The FBM Emas declined 148.49 points, or 1.21%, to 12,143.53, while the FBM Shariah lost 163.34 points, or 1.34%, to 12,013.01.  Heavyweight counters were mostly lower. Maybank slipped four sen to RM9.95, Public Bank fell three sen to RM4.67 and CIMB shed 10 sen to RM7.69. Tenaga Nasional declined six sen to RM12.90, while IHH Healthcare lost 13 sen to RM7.70.  Among the most actively traded stocks, Zetrix AI Bhd added 0.5 sen to 16.5 sen on 188.38 million shares, while VS Industry Bhd fell one sen to 27 sen.  JAKS Resources Bhd dropped 2.5 sen to 18 sen, newly ACE Market listed GB Bond Holdings Bhd slid 4.5 sen to 20.5 sen, while HHRG Bhd gained 0.5 sen to 16.5 sen.  Trading activity eased, with turnover falling to 3.1 billion units worth RM2.7 billion, from 3.63 billion units valued at RM3.62 billion on Sept 30.
